utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you were questioning Mr. Lukac?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, before the witness returns to the witness box, I just wanted to touch on something we raised yesterday when your Honour was asking me about the length of the trial. I do not think I really probably explained the basis of our calculation. We have calculated two witnesses per day on a five day week when we did the calculation. That was 40 per month and then in eight weeks we would cover 80 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Wait now, tell me again, two what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Two witnesses per day on a five-day week which is 10 witnesses a week.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: On your list sometimes you have a witness for a day; with Dr. Gow, you had one to two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do expect, your Honour, some days to have three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, you go ahead. Tell me how you calculated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So our calculation was basically two witnesses a day, five days a week, which is 40 witnesses a month, and over an eight week period is 80 witnesses, and we said six to nine weeks. If you add an extra week, that allows for 90 witnesses. We just cannot be sure that all witnesses that we have put in our list will give evidence at this stage. This is our best estimate. So our calculation initially of six to nine weeks is still, on that basis of calculation, accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Six to nine witnesses -- I am slow, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Six to nine weeks. Our calculation of six to nine weeks when you calculate it that way is still accurate, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That would be how many witnesses per week?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 10 witnesses a week. That is the average.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, 10 witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Per week.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have 88 witnesses, for sure, that you will call. If you have 10 witnesses a week, with 88, you would have eight, nine weeks, I guess; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is "will call", but then you have also 46 "may call" so that would be another four or four and a half weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that happens, but it is very unlikely that we will call them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except that once again -- maybe we added the time wrong; you help me -- on the 88 witnesses, you did not have necessarily two per day, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Some of the witnesses in the early stages we have said may take a whole day, and we will put that in, but we are averaging it out; on some days we anticipate to have three. If we have three witnesses, that will catch up and balance it out.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not have the time with me, it is not really important and it really was not my concern that you had told the Trial Chamber six to nine weeks and now you were taking additional time. That is not the concern. It was just the math of just adding up the hours and adding up the hours of the "will call". I must admit I left that. Regardless of how much time you told us you were going to use, regardless whether if you add up the 88 witnesses and the number of hours that you have listed, whether that comes to six months or four months, the question is what can we do, if anything, to make sure that we are using our time efficiently? Since we are talking about it, maybe I can explore it a little bit more with you. I had suggested, we had suggested, that perhaps you meet with Defence in an effort to see what could be done to organise the case more tightly. You had indicated that there had been at least some discussions about perhaps entering into stipulations. What the Chamber would like to suggest very strongly is that you meet with Defence, that the Defence meet with the Prosecution on this Friday, or at least at some point before Monday of next week, in an effort to attempting to shorten the trial, not to cut it off, but to make it as efficient as possible. You have listed 14 policy witnesses after Mr. Lukac -- this is my math -- and those 14 policy witnesses, a maximum would require 65 hours. We work about five hours a day, it is about five and a half, but sometimes we are late getting started, so that would be 13 days maximum that you would use for those 14 policy witnesses. I understand what you just told me that you were assuming two witnesses a day. I am telling you what the math shows; at least for 14 policy witnesses is a maximum 65 hours, 13 days. That would not be two witnesses a day obviously. Minimum would be 8.8 days and that is not two witnesses a day. So what we are suggesting is that perhaps with those witnesses, particularly, you consider offering their statements only and then presenting them for cross-examination, the statements would be received into evidence -- I have not seen the statements, I do not know how full they are -- then you, of course, would have the opportunity for redirect for whatever reasons you may consider appropriate. Again we do not know what it is that you intend to offer by way of the policy witnesses, we have just heard from one, we have not finished hearing from Mr. Lukac, but that is a possibility. Again are not directing you, we are just focusing in and without knowing your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is very difficult for us to do it that way. I mean, there are a number of problems with this. Firstly, we are most loathe to approach the Defence and ask them whether or not they wish to make any admissions. We are loathe to do that because we consider that as putting pressure on the Defence, and their counsel may now agree with it, but if there is a change of counsel, there is an appeal, unless the accused is very sure of this, this is something which we, the Prosecution, are most reluctant to do, put pressure on. If the Defence approach us, as I have said, the door is open and we are happy. So, if the Defence come to us, that is fine, we are very happy to speak to them, but we are must reluctant to approach them. The second thing, your Honours, is that if a matter is in dispute and it is clearly in dispute, this is the first time that one of these cases has been prosecuted; we just do not know the parameters of what is required in terms of proof. So to proceed in a way that is suggested by your Honour may well fall short of what is required; it may not, it may be sufficient but we just do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am not asking you not to put on evidence. I am suggesting that there is a possible alternative to putting on 14 policy witnesses. I am not in any way suggesting that you do not need to; I am just throwing this out as a suggestion. You can look at the policy witnesses, see whether you have to actually call them all for direct testimony or whether, perhaps, instead you could offer the statements. The Defence could then cross-examine and you would have an opportunity on redirect. Then you have 39, I think, witnesses for count 1 with a maximum of 146 hours, that is 29.2 days. We are getting closer now to two witnesses, I guess -- no, we are not still, but in any case, let me suggest that you meet. Are you saying that you do not even want to meet with Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not at all. I am saying we are must reluctant to approach the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I am approaching the Defence and asking the Defence to meet with the Prosecutor at some point between now and Monday morning. We will not be meeting on this case on Friday. I would suggest that is a good day. I do not know what your availability is on Friday, but at least sit down and see whether this is a possibility. Before you tell me no absolutely, at least think about it. This is the first that you have heard about the suggestion that, perhaps, you offer statements from some of the policy witnesses even. So, I would encourage you not to just absolutely foreclose as soon as you hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would never do that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let it sink in a little bit and kind of let it roll around for a while before you say no absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour. We will certainly take that and give it very, very serious consideration.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will the Defence, Mr. Wladimiroff, meet with the Prosecutor between Wednesday and Monday to discuss the direction of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not sure we are able to comply with that suggestion of the court. I think we have to consider within the team because we see some complications here. I mean, if the Prosecution will present the statements as evidence and we will cross-examine the witness on that evidence, we are not sure whether the witness would have repeated under oath what is in his statement there. So we have to consider very carefully each statement, whether we could accept that. I am not sure it is within the limits we have set out for the Defence so we have to discuss that. The second problem might be that we are not complete during Friday, no -- on Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday we are not all complete, so I am not sure whether we are able to comply with this suggestion. It seems to the Prosecution that we have to make the first move. I have to think about that too.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think I have made the first move.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution is not going to approach us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have approached you for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have suggested a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will not be altogether; is that what you are saying, Thursday, Friday, Saturday or Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, that is correct. We will give very good thought. We will certainly discuss it tonight and let us see how far we can come, but I am not in a position now to promise that we will be able and willing to meet with Prosecution on this issue, but we will try to find a solution, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann? Would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour. Might Mr. Lukac be brought in, please? MR. DRAGAN LUKAC, recalled Examination continued by MR. NIEMANN.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you allow me? We have this computer, we try to work with it, but we have no mouse today. I asked already the computer should be installed. I do not know whether this can be quickly; if I so, I would highly appreciate it to be done. I asked already the person who seems to be responsible for the computers to get me one, but he went away and did not come back. So if it can be solved quickly, I would be very glad if it would be solved; if not, then of course we will do without.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: My colleague says that he is coming down. (To the witness): Mr. Lukac, I understand that you are still under oath. You took an oath yesterday and you understand you are still under that oath? (The witness nods in the affirmative).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Lukac, yesterday towards the end of your evidence you were telling us how you were taken to Brcko and you were there around the end of April, early May. On 2nd May at about 4.30 in the afternoon, were you then taken out to a bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In translation]: The 2nd May 1992, we were informed by the military police which guarded the prison that we would be transferred to the military prison in the Bijeljina barracks. In the afternoon, sometime in the afternoon, we were taken out and put on a bus which then set off to Bijeljina. It was guarded by two army vehicles, by two APCs, with JNA members. After we arrived at the barracks in Bijeljina, at the prison, we were taken out to the pista, to that pista where soldiers usually gather. We were told to raise our arms, put them behind our heads and align ourselves. Now, along that strip of land, that pista, there were two tanks and they were manned with men on them, and one was who was detained in Brcko and he was brought there while he was a Muslim. He was told to step out of the column and to move in the opposite direction, that is, from the direction that we were moving in and he did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to this man then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed then because the machine gun was open from the tanks and he was shot there on the spot without an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the tanks, JNA tanks, so far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were JNA tanks and the barracks also belonged to JNA in that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The barracks at Bijeljina, they were JNA barracks, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were at Bijeljina in the JNA barracks, were you beaten or otherwise mistreated during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately upon our arrival we were taken to the gym which is within the barracks, on the premises of the barracks, and we were ordered to sit down on the floor and then members of the military police immediately began to mistreat us. They beat us with different objects, kicked us with feet, with rifle butts, rifles they had with them, and it lasted all day until about 23, 2400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 3rd May 1992 did some JNA officers enter the room where you were and call out a list of names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 3rd May some time in the afternoon a group of JNA officers entered that gymnasium hall that we were in and said that they would read out some names, and that those whose names were read should move to the opposite side of that gymnasium where we were. Then they read out six names. It was six of us of whom Simo Zaric while we were in Brcko, in the prison in Brcko, had told that we were treated as political prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then taken out into the middle of a field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were then ordered again to put our hands behind our heads and to come out of the gymnasium one by one. We did that. We were escorted by military police and that group of JNA officers who also followed. When we came out, we followed a path which goes by the building of the barracks taking into a football field, a soccer field, which is also within the barracks of the JNA in Bijeljina. In the middle of that soccer field was a JNA helicopter and it was already switched off. I remember that the propeller was moving, I remember the detail, and next to it there were also some, a group of JNA officers. We were then taken to this helicopter and we were ordered to board it which we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once you had boarded the helicopter can you tell me who was in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we boarded it, we found the three men from Bosanski Samac who were sitting on a bench in that helicopter. In the middle of the helicopter was a coffin covered with a Serbian flag, and in it was a member of Grey Wolves paramilitary formation, and we knew him in Brcko because he used to come to the prison where we were kept, and a JNA policeman. So that after that a civilian also boarded and, in all likelihood, it was a member, a JNA or a Kos, K-O-S, member. Then we were chained together, nine of us, and then the helicopter took off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see where you were going when you took off in the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the windows of the helicopter we could see the ground below, yes, in the direction of the flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able ultimately to determine where you were going by looking out of the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know at first, but after some time I realised we were flying over the Sava River and then after some time more I recognised the town below us, it was the town called Sremska Mitrovica, because I had been to that town on several occasions and I knew it, I could recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is Sremska Mitrovica, in what republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sremska Mitrovica is in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did the helicopter ultimately land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the flight took some more time and then again out of the window I saw that we were above a military airport. It was a rather large army complex, military complex, and down on the runway there were a number of fighter planes and military helicopters. So our helicopter landed on the grass field, that is not on the runway, but the grass beside it. Then we were told to get off the helicopter. It was very difficult to do it because we were all chained together. But when I got up I saw that the helicopter was surrounded by very many JNA military police, and they were not wearing SMB uniforms, but light blue of the Air Force uniforms, but they were still wearing the white belts of the military police. Then we were ordered to lie down facing to the earth, presumably, not to look and observe this military complex. I guess that was the reason. Then we boarded a JNA truck. It was covered with canvas, and after a short ride of about five minutes we were again told to get off, whereupon we were taken to a cellar, to underground premises of a facility and when we got there we realised it was a prison because there were bars on the main door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we had spent some time in that prison, they took off the handcuffs off our hands, and before that a JNA officer came into the cell. He was a captain, a rank. After sometime he asked us if we had any questions, and I asked him if he could tell us where we were. He told us: "You are with the Yugoslav People's Army", and I said that I realised that, but I wondered what locality the site and he told me: "This is enough".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you personally when you were there kept in detention at this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first three days of our stay in that prison cell, from 5 o'clock in the morning to 10 o'clock in the evening we had to stand to attention aligned in rows, and on a third day or so, the military police, whose various guards requested us to sing songs with Chetnik lyrics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you taught these songs or were these songs that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not know the text, the lyrics. They told us what were the lyrics and then we sing them in a chorus and trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to making you sing songs, did they make you do anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the wall of this prison room there was a drawing of Draza Mihailovic. Draza Mihailovic was a Chetnik leader, was a Chetnik leader from the Second World War. From time to time we were put in a column one by one and they ordered us to kiss the drawing of Draza Mihailovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they do anything to you concerning your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also after some time in that prison room, the military policemen asked us to learn how to make the sign of a cross in the orthodox way. The sign of the cross is made in a different way in the orthodox religion than in the Catholic religion, because the orthodox use three fingers whereas the Catholics use the whole hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to people who refused to do these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody tried to refuse to do it because simply everyone knew what would happen, that means the beatings. All of us from time to time in the next couple of days learned how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then later discover the name of the place where you were, the name of the military establishment that you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the next couple of days from the military policemen that guarded us and who changed every three hours, we learned from them that we were at the JNA barracks at Batajnica. Batajnica is a town very near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look now, please, at this map that I show you? (Handed) Just by looking at the map itself, can you tell me what that map shows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map shows the north eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a part of the Republic of Serbia as well as a part of the Republic of Croatia, that is, the eastern part of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that map, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has Defence seen the map and what number would it be and do you have an extra copy for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 72, your Honour. I did give a copy to the Defence, your Honour. Perhaps that might be marked and handed to the witness? With the assistance of Miss Sutherland, I will ask that the map be displayed on the projector, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No objection to Defence 72?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I just have a glance at it so I can recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, please show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No objection to ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- Prosecution 72 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Mr. Lukac, would you please with the pointer show us where Bosanski Samac is on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosanski Samac is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That green line immediately above Bosanski Samac, do you recognise that , what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The green line marks the border between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In your evidence you said you went from Bosanski Samac to Brcko. Can you show us Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Then you said you were taken to Bijeljina, can you show us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Then it is at Bijeljina you boarded a helicopter. Can you show us approximately the route that the helicopter followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you the exact route, but I remember one bit when we were flying over the River Sava. The River Sava is along the border between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, and later on between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, so somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where did you go from there, after you crossed the border into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably this way, because I told you I remember very well that we flew over the town of Sremska Mitrovica which is here and we arrived to Batajnica which is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is the place that you just described a moment ago in your evidence where you were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Perhaps the exhibit might be returned, if your Honours please? On 12th May in the early afternoon were you then gathered up and ordered to board a truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 12th May in the cell where we were entered a group of officers, of JNA officers. Among them was the first class captain which I mentioned when I spoke about our arrival to that prison, and while we were in that prison we learned that he was a security officer at the JNA barracks at Batajnica. They carried with us four camouflage uniforms worn by JNA soldiers without no rank insignia. From nine of us that were in there, they chose four of us and told us to put on those uniforms. After that they handcuffed us and they put white bandages around our eyes. After that they took us out of the prison and they put us on a military truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you then driven in the truck for sometime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The drive lasted for some 30 to 40 minutes, and after that the vehicle pulled down and we were told to get off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise the place where you had arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not recognise the place because we were blindfolded with white bandages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: After the blindfolds were taken off and so forth, were you later then told by a captain where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we were taken into a room and the blinds were taken off, so that I noticed that we were in a room which was a school room of the JNA barracks because they all look alike. After some half an hour, a captain, a JNA captain, entered the room and he told us we were at the barracks of the military police in Zemun. Zemun is a city very near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you later find out why you had been brought to this place and why you had been required to dress in this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were there nobody told us why we were brought there, but we managed to conclude that we had probably been brought there in order to be filmed for the Belgrade TV and probably shown wearing those uniforms as members of either the Croatian or Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: After going to this place where were you then taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 14th May, that means four years ago to this day, we were handcuffed again and blindfolded and we were taken back to the Batajnica prison where we were held before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: How long were you then held at the Batajnica prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the Batajnica prison we remained until 26th May 1992 when in our prison arrived three members of that Fourth Detachment from Bosanski Samac. We were told that out of the nine of us four were to go back with them to Bosanski Samac and I was among those four people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you then taken back to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were handcuffed and blindfolded again and then with a van we were taken back to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What happened to you when you got back to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon our arrival to Bosanski Samac, we were taken into the yard of the police station, and after that the four of us were imprisoned in one of the garages that is in that yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: For how long were you then imprisoned in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this first period in that garage, as far as I can remember, we were there up until 23rd June, and after that we were transferred to the prison cells in the police Station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: During the time you were in Bosanski Samac, either in the garage or in the prison cells, how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were treated very cruelly in the same way as they treated us during the first phase that we spent at Bosanski Samac. We were abused, we lived in very difficult conditions, especially in that garage because in there the floor was concrete, we had nothing to sleep on, just two blankets for the four of us. The food was very bad. Especially after some 10 days upon our arrival, we received only one meal per day, and that meal contained a piece of bread large as a cigarette box and with some marmalade over it. That is what we had to eat for the next 70 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: During that time did you lose weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in the camp and in those prisons I lost 30 kilos. I left prison with 70 kilos and before the war began I had exactly 100 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the cells for, up until what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that cell in which we were imprisoned in the first place there were two people per each cell, and on 4th July 1992 two people were exchanged, so there were just two of us left there. We were practically in a solitary cell for some 60 days and we were exchanged on 4th September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exchange took place on the motorway Zagreb/Belgrade near the town Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who supervised the exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The supervision was done by the UNPROFOR members and by the representatives of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Lukac, in the course of your evidence yesterday you were telling us about the paramilitary groups and I think you mentioned the Seselj paramilitary groups. Were there, to your knowledge, any other paramilitary groups operational in the area of Bosanski Samac at the beginning and during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the knowledge I had of the situation, this paramilitary group that since the beginning of the war, that is, the occupation of our municipality, was on the territory of our municipality, that particular group belonged to Seselj's units. I was certain about that in the month of October 1992 when I read in a Serbian newspaper called The Telegraph, I read there an interview with Slobodan Miljkovic, called "Lugar", who belonged to these units and this Tribunal has got an indictment against this person, and that person said in that interview very precisely that he and his men belonged to the units of Vojislav Seselj, that is, they belonged to the radical party from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Had he belonged to any other paramilitary group, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same interview he states that previously he used to belong to Arkan's units and that he had been trained in a camp of Arkan's soldiers in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Once you were exchanged and were released, did you then proceed to have a medical check-up upon your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I left the prison, I had a medical check up and a number of injuries were stated at that check-up that I got while I was in the prisons in Bosanski Samac or in the prisons of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What were the injuries that you suffered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was found that I had some fractures of the skull, eight teeth were broken, my ribs on the right-hand side were broken, my right kidney had been damaged; my sight deteriorated. These were the most important damages to my health with some minor injuries that accompanied that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukac, you are excused. Any objections to Mr. Lukac been permanently excused? Mr. Lukac, you are excused permanently. Thank you for coming. Mr. Niemann, would you like to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I call Sulejman Tihic. SULEJMAN TIHIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Sulejman Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 26th November 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born at Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you live there all of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attend university at Sarajevo where you graduated with a degree in law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you work as a judge for four years and as an attorney for four years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was also a public Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you for some time have your own private practice as a lawyer in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was an attorney for nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I belong to the Islamic religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, at the start of the war were you involved in politics in Bosanski Samac district?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I participated as the chairman of the party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what that particular party represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the political life of the town and of our region, and even more in Bosnia and Herzegovina, participated on a voluntary basis, not on a professional basis, and that party represented the interests of the Bosniac, that is at that time the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you also President of the Town Assembly in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Town Assembly and at some stage I was also the President of the Town Assembly. I would like to say that it was the town not the whole municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These positions that you are speaking of, are they elected positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To all the functions I held, I held them after the elections where I was chosen among many candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you been involved with the SDA since August 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were elected President in September 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you become a member of the National Committee of the SDA for all of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the highest representative body, the political body, yes, that was the main committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What responsibilities and duties did you have as a consequence of your political office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I held almost all the office in the town, starting from the President of the Fire Brigade Association, then the President of the Town Assembly and in the municipality I was one of the members of that Assembly. I was a member of the Security Council in the Dobje region which contains nine municipalities. I was the Deputy Chairman of the Party of Democratic Action for that region, and for the Party of the Democratic Action I was part of this main national Council, and also the chairman of the Council for legal questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What responsibilities and duties did you have when you worked for the Council for Security of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that all my offices were political. I did that on a voluntary basis, that is, my responsibility was primarily political towards those people that elected me. In this Council for Security, we were discussing the issues that would be of the interests of all the three nationalities that lived at Bosanski Samac. We were trying to solve interethnical issues, that is, the attentions or incidents that may have arised. Partly we succeeded, but, as you know, we were not able to prevent the clash itself. As far as we in Samac was concerned, maybe that conflict could have been prevented had it not been for the outside intervention, everything directed from that centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you talk of outside intervention, to what are you referring, in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about the so-called Yugoslav People's Army. Had it not been for it and for the weapons that it had distributed to only one nationality, it is sure that that particular nationality would have been more ready to negotiate with the Muslims and the Croats, and the conflict could have been avoided because it is difficult if they have all the weapons and we do not have anything, they do not want to negotiate, they want to do only the way they want to do things. The army was on their side 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What nationality are you referring to when you say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army was on the side of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say you worked with representatives of each of the groups in order to resolve interethnic disputes, what particular groups, political groups in particular, are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked for the Security Council in our Assembly with the Serb Democratic Party and its President, Blagoje Simic, Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, Pavo Catic, the SDP, the former Communist reformers, Liberals; we all worked in a body and we were trying to solve the problems in our life. I co-operated with everybody. They were all my party, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, we all visited each other for religious holidays on the Christmas or Bayram almost until the day of arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke earlier of the JNA. Do you recall an organisation referred as the Fourth Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Fourth Detachment was a part of the JNA that they belonged to its organisational structure. I know that because the Fourth Detachment, their Commander and Deputy Commander, in a way took part in all of the meetings we had in town trying to forestall the conflict, and the Commander of, I believe, the 17th Tactical Group, which is part of the JNA of Brcko garrison, he also attended our sessions and represented the Fourth Detachment as being their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the Commander and Deputy Commander of the Fourth Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander was Radovan Antic and Deputy, Simo Zaric, although in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the Commander of the 17th Tactical group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Stefan Nikolic. He was also Deputy Commander of the JNA barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1990, I think you just touched on this a moment ago in your evidence, did the JNA take away the weapons from the local Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I believe it was May 1990 they took away the weapons from Territorial Defence. I think they also did it in Samac, and I also heard about it, I think, I am not quite sure, I am not positive, but it also happened in the barracks in Davinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was this received, this action received, in the local community in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment when these weapons were taken away, these decisions are implemented overnight. The democracy was not at such level one could protest or react to this because the JNA was still so powerful at the time that nobody even dared think that they could do something against it, and all this was done very quickly; so that people did remonstrate and were against it, but there was no organised protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was technically responsible for the arming and controlling arms of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Keep your voice up, please, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, your Honour. (To the witness): Who was technically responsible for the arming and controlling of arms of territorial defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was under the jurisdiction of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, the authorities of the Republic starting with presidency to regional, to local authorities, and various companies were responsible for the arming of the Territorial Defence and they set aside resources for the financing of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With respect to the creation of the Fourth Detachment in the area, how was this received by the local community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local population and all politically organised forces, that is, parties with the exception of SDS, this was not received as well. We thought that the JNA was taking over the functions, the task of the Territorial Defence, probably fearing that it would have sufficient influence on the Territorial Defence, and thus, it to a certain extent paralysed the Territorial Defence because the Fourth Detachment was nothing else in terms of the organisation and work. It functioned as the Territorial Defence, but it fell under the jurisdiction of JNA rather than the Republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your assistance sought by the JNA in terms of the establishment of this Fourth Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean directly, no, they did not ask any our assistance when establishing the Fourth Detachment. They did it on their own first secretly and then they admitted it at the Assembly, but later they tried to win our support to this Fourth Detachment. I, as the President of the local SDS, was contacted personally and they tried it also with other political parties. However, we refused. We wanted those men of the Fourth Detachment to join the Territorial Defence on an equal footing with all the others who already were in the Territorial Defence, but Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic and men around him refused to accept it precisely because in that manner they would lose the command over that detachment. As I have said, the Territorial Defence was under the local, that is, republican authorities, republican presidency; whereas JNA and the Fourth detachment were under the command of the army, that is, Chief of Staff etc., all those in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did the Commander of the JNA, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, do in relation to yourself concerning the Fourth Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He once invited me, he asked me to come to their command outpost at Obudovac for a talk. I received a message through Simo Zaric and I informed about it. The executive board of the party for Democratic Action has said I would not go alone, and we set up a delegation which was also made of Izet, Izet Izetbegovic, and we went to Obudovac for talks, but when they saw that Izet was present there, I believe they renounced some intentions, some intent, to try to persuade me and we talked about the JNA which controlled the entry points into town, the access to the bridge and the police and local authorities should be suspended. But we refused that proposal and we discussed that and some other matters. We, perhaps, talked about preventing the conflict and then returned to Samac. I could see that they were not very happy to see Izet, Izet Izetbegovic, come with me and I believe they changed the topic because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic discussed with you the question of surrendering control of the Bosanski Samac bridge into Bosanski Samac which up until this stage had been under the control of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have just said that. He asked that this patrol, that his patrol, takes a point of traffic some 200 or 300 metres away from the bridges, and that they should control all of the entries and exits from Bosnia, that is, everything that enter the territory of Bosnia and exited from the territory of Bosnia. We refused it because we thought that there were regular police Forces and that this was within their jurisdiction, and that under the constitution and by Statute the army had absolutely no jurisdiction over this because there was no state of war and, therefore, we resisted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: About a month before the commencement of the war in April 1992, did you observe things happening in or about Bosanski Samac, especially with respect to the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it happened that JNA garrison in Brcko pulled out almost all the weaponry and all the soldiers and they were deployed in Serb villages around Samac. They were digging in, building trenches and distributing weapons among the Serb population as a kind of mobilization, I do not know, and they took up some positions and that caused, gave rise, to anxiety, to concern, among others, non-Serb people, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the non-Serb people do anything to try to defend themselves during this period leading up to 17th April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, since, if I may say so, fear began to set in seeing some being armed officially or semi-officially, at least. Even in towns Serbs (sic) were given no weapons through the Fourth Detachment. So non-Serb peoples or, rather, members of non-Serb peoples also tried to find their way about. Some people bought some weapons and, as a political party, of course, we also addressed the question. We tried to activate the Territorial Defence, but that was difficult because the Territorial Defence had no weaponry apart from the list and registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The translation that I see on our screen here says that Serbs were given no weapons through the Fourth Detachment; did you say Serbs were given no weapons or non-Serbs were given no weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Non-Serbs did not get weapons, Serbs did, whether from the Fourth Detachment or the JNA, and we tried, Croats and Bosniacs, the only way to look after their security was to do it through reserve militia. We mobilized the reserve militia force which the Serbs did not want to join, and we tried to ensure, to provide, security in the town, access roads, the bridge, and to work through those legal structures to arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What weaponry was available at this time to the non-Serb population who tried to set up some sort of defence capability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those were automatic and there were some hunting rifles, carabins again, shotguns, no heavy weaponry. One could not even imagine it; I could not imagine that one could have that or even buy it or get it, perhaps a bomb here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Leading up to the time just prior to the commencement of the war, what role did the members of the Fourth Detachment play in and about Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the role of the Fourth Detachment was to prevent the organisation of any defence and resistance in the town of Bosanski Samac. It was mostly concentrated in the town. At first they organised propaganda saying that they were part of the JNA which belonged equally to Serbs, Croats and Bosniacs, and try to involve some Croats and Bosniacs, and some of them did join because in Bosnia, especially JNA, was held in high esteem. It was highly appreciated as a force which was common to all, and until a few years ago many people did not feel the changes and, therefore, some of them were misguided and joined the Fourth Detachment. But when they realised the true intentions of this Fourth Detachment, many left it and finally it became the Fourth Detachment of the Serb people. They patrolled the town, they held the levies, the banks, pretended they were guarding and taking care that the Croats from the neighbouring Croatia do not make any incursion. There were sometimes conflicts with the reserve militia from time to time in the town itself, because there were some ruffians, some thugs, in the Fourth Detachment, people behaving violently, and they sometimes used to carry their weapons around the town and even fire them. But the purpose was to prevent any other organised defence. I think that was the principal raison d'etre, the principal purpose, even though they were saying they were there to defend us from a possible incursion from the Croatian side which was not a real danger and there were no such attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just prior to the commencement of the war in Bosanski Samac or the attack on Bosanski Samac, were you informed about the existence of paramilitary units and can you tell us how it is that you became to be informed of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was informed from different sources by different people that representatives of part of these paramilitary forces were arriving or were in the town, and one of my clients of Serb ethnic origin from Obudovac came to me and they called, they addressed the lawyers as "doctors", and he said: "Doctor, a JNA helicopter has landed with those in red berets", and he said there were about 20 of them. He said they were at Obudovac. They were very violent; that they had tried to rape some women; that local Serb patrol which was somewhere on the border with Croatia got drunk in a pub together with them because they knew that they caught that patrol and they beat them and shaved their heads because they were long haired, and he said that they came, that a JNA helicopter brought them in, and that in the village there they were already trying to rape women and causing various trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the area of Bosanski Samac which was the first town to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an attack on Modrica but it did not last long, a day or two, and then the legal authority was re-established, but after that or before that it was Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you recall the night that Bosanski Samac was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can. That night, rather, on the eve of the attack, we had a meeting among people, representatives of the Fourth Detachment, we had representatives of SDS, of HDZ, I represented SDA, there were representatives of reformers and ex-Communists, and Simo Zaric on behalf of the Fourth Detachment, subsequently we were told he was to join us later because he was at consultation with Colonel Nikolic in Brcko. So we waited for him and when he came were planning that meeting, and we had agreed to bring together, to unite, to merge, the American the Fourth Department and the Territorial Defence. But Simo, when he came back from that meeting in Brcko, refused any possibility, any prospect, of joint detachment. Beforehand, I think he was ready to compromise and go along with that, but after returning from Brcko he refused it flatly, and then I began to doubt, to suspect, that something could happen because he was not ready to make any compromises. After the meeting, we went to a pub for a drink and then again we heard stories that Samac would be attacked, but they were frequent, and I simply did not take it seriously. I went home and around 2 o'clock I heard the fire shots. I looked out of the window and in my yard I saw the members of the Fourth Detachment. We already knew them more or less. In the morning I was at home and when day broke out, I tried, I went to a neighbour who was Serb together with my wife, my sister, my brother and my sister-in-law. From there I moved to my colleague, Borisav Pisarevic, because I risked to be killed in the house of this Serb, and I thought that Boro was more eminent, more prestigious, among Serbs that he could protect me and perhaps take me out of the town. In the afternoon, Boro came to fetch me. He came with his car and took me and my wife, and I stayed with him for a day, and since he lived on the fourth floor, we watched what was happening in the town, shots, the fire (indecipherable). I think that the fire was at random. There were organised resistance because at the moment of the attack, the Fourth Detachment came out in the streets, took the key positions, cut off telephones and those paramilitary formations and the Serb Territorial Defence, attacked at the police -- I do not know, do you want me to go into detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At any rate -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is just one matter about the translation that I saw. I think you said there was armed resistance; did you say there was armed resistance or no armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Armed resistance existed when the militia was attacked and a part of the citizens of Samac came out with weapons to the centre of the town. There were some shots, there were some resistance. Around 10 or 11, there was a group of people more or less organised at resisting, but when JNA tanks and the armed cars of the JNA entered the town, people realised that it was hope against hope, and they returned home or went to another village, to a neighbouring village, a Croat village, near Bosanski Samac. If there was any armed resistance it existed only until the entry of JNA tanks and then it ceased and people scattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you? Were you, did you leave the town? Did you stay there? What happened to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night I spent with Boro and next day Boro was trying through some connections to get me out of the town. He called Simo Zaric and others. I knew Simo Zaric. He was the head of Security and I was the regional Prosecutor; we had known each other for 15 years through the judiciary and the police, and we tried to get him to take me out of the town, but nothing happened. He did not answer the telephone. The next day a member of the paramilitary formations came, I do not know if they were Grey Wolves or, and a local policeman and arrested Boro and me and took us to the police. There I found Kapetan Crni who asked me to make a statement for radio to invite the people not to resist. While I was in the corridor, when I came out, Miljkovic, "Lugar", that is, he asked me if I was the President of SDA. I said "yes" and then he beat me and several others also started hitting me. They took me to the radio and I there made a statement which they had written for me to read. After that they detained me in the SUP. They immediately started harassing me, beating me, and it lasted. In Bosanski Samac especially, there were so many formations, so many uniforms, armies, Arkan's men, the Grey Wolves, Red Berets and whoever came here would start looking for the more important people, for the principal ones, and they would ask for these chiefs, and I was one of those. So they battered us and they beat us. First, they used the police truncheons, then they all got broke, so they picked up whatever they could find and they hit us with whatever they could lay their hands on. We were forced to sing songs. We kept singing those Chetniks songs belittling Croats and Muslims and emphasising Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to the radio station what was the message that you had to read out over the radio when you were taken to the radio station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to invite the citizens of Samac not to resist those units which had occupied Samac, that was the first thing, and to tell them that their security was guaranteed and that the Serb authorities would treat correctly and that nothing bad would happen to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do this of your own free will or were you under force to do this, to read this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not of my own free will. Of course, I had to read it and it was not a journalist, it was one of Arkan's men who interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you gave this broadcast over the radio what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then that Arkan's men told me to go home. I understood then from the memorial centre, and so JNA APC there and some soldiers, and I remember before I went to the radio station that Captain Crni to take me back, and it sounded curious that this one said go home. I immediately suspected they wanted to kill me, that I would move and they would shoot then. But while I was thinking about that, a journalist who was there came down and switched the recording device, and he asked them to take him home in the police car, and I seized the opportunity and also entered that car. After that they took me to the SUP and for a while I was detained in the SUP building, and two Arkan's men interrogated me, beat me and even called a girl in Belgrade and that girl ostensibly asked what were you doing, and her boyfriend would turn, they said towards me while I would say: "Well, I am hitting" and his girlfriend was listening to what to what he was doing. Then they took me to the storage room of the Territorial Defence and I found there another 50 men or so, mostly Croats and Bosniacs. Then two or three days later they started with interrogation, mostly by Simo Zaric, the Deputy Commander of the Fourth Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At some stage did they offer to allow you to leave if you paid a sum of money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, it is very difficult to describe the situation in a very short time. They were just coming, beating, killing, there was -- it was incomprehensible, beyond understanding. There was another Lazar Stanisic, a friend of mine who was a Serb. I asked him whether he could help me. He told me: "You have to give 20,000 Deutschemarks to the captain called Crni, and there might be a possibility for him to release you". I told him then: "My brother is at Kladanj. Telephone him, tell him that and he will bring the money", and after that Lava left. We were transferred to Brcko, and when Lazar came to Brcko I asked him whether my brother brought the money. He said: "Yes, he did. Everything is going to be fine, you are going to be released", but to no avail because they only took the money. They did not let me go. After that I realised, I learned from my brother they did not ask for 20,000,000 Deutschemark but 15,000 Deutschemarks. I do not know whether they changed that, 15,000 Deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you at any stage ask Simo Zaric why you were being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were interrogating me, I asked why I was detained and he said in order not to organise some kind of resistance, that was some kind of preventative detention, and that I would soon be released in a couple of days. That is what he had promised me, but I do not know whether he was lying or whether he was not able to release me, because all the others were involved that he had to ask in order that I could be released, but they did not release anyone, two or three persons, all the rest continued to be detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did then subsequently Simo Zaric come and tell you that you were going into the army or going with the army, I should say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He only told me that the army was going to come to pick us up and take us out of Bosanski Samac, because in those 10 days we were so much beaten that it was a question of a day or two, if they continued to beat us at the same peace, we were all going to be killed from the beatings. We were full of bruises. Captain Petrovic from the army, the Chief of the Security from Brcko, came to take us. I knew him from before the war because he used to come to Samac. He came with two trucks. They loaded us on the trucks and they brought us to the barracks of Brcko. When the soldiers saw us at Brcko, they told us later on they were prepared to beat us, but when they saw in which way we looked, how hard we were -- how hardly we could walk, they decided not to beat us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Tihic, if I may, I would like to take you back just a moment to something you said in the course of your evidence before the break. When I was asking you about the arms that were available to the non-Serbs that were setting up some form of defence, you mentioned rifles etc., you also said maybe a bomb. Can you assist us in what you were talking about with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arms that were available to the non-Serbian population were the arms that were at the police -- the station of Public Security, and then we also tried to organise something, and so we had some 25 automatic rifles, and there was also a box with some 10 or so grenades. We distributed this to the members of our party which acknowledged the receipt of those weapons and when necessary they patrol, that is, they guarded the entrance and the exits to the town during the night where we had information that Samac would be attacked, but these were all old automatic weapons from the Second World War. I think they used to call them "kenca" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Moving up into 26th and 27th April, I think you were then with a group of other people taken to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at Brcko what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Brcko, they first of all unloaded us, if I can use that expression, and then the military policemen searched each and every one of us. They took all our valuable possessions that we still had and that had not been taken away from us in Samac. To me, personally, they took away my watch and some 150 to 200 Swiss Francs, my driving licence and a ring. After that they put us in various rooms. Myself and three other people, I think Dragan Lukac, Osman Jasarevic and Grga Zubak, we spent the night in a separate room. They told us that was a room what they called for the extremists and we had to sleep handcuffed. We were not really able to sleep because constantly people were coming in and showing us as we were some kind of monsters. Then the next day we were transferred to the room with other prisoners and the handcuffs were taken off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was this establishment that you were taken to in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was, those were military barracks in Brcko. Brcko are 50 kilometres from Samac. I used to go there quite often because I had family there and also on official business as an attorney. I know the way those barracks look and I was imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was a JNA barracks, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA barracks, of course. The rooms where we were were the rooms that used to belong to some kind of a prison because they had those kinds of bars that you find in prisons and all the other things that are usually to be found in prisons. There were military police there and the members of the army. It is true some members of the paramilitary groups would also come in, they will threaten us that they would kill us, also the red berets and so on, but they would not beat us at Brcko and they were not allowed to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you distinguish between the JNA soldiers, the paramilitaries and the police that were at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA soldiers used to wear the uniform that we all knew from the previous JNA. We all knew what this uniform looked like because it had the five pointed star, then the greenish uniform, everyone knew about this type of uniform, but all the others had other types of insignia. For example, the four S letters. I saw that all the Wolves wore it the other way round from the usual way you find those four Ss. Then there were other Chetnik insignia. Usually, we call them special type of soldiers because they had sort of camouflage uniforms in various colours, whereas the JNA wore this olivey green type of uniforms, and also the army soldiers were usually younger people, neatly with a neat hair cut, whereas the others were older people, ugly with beards and so on, and they were wearing things that would create a feeling of fear, for example, skulls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the police, how did you determine which ones were the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military policemen had white belts and that was the way one could recognise a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you touched on the fact that they seemed to be all working in together, is that correct, these three groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They operated together. They attacked Samac together. First of all, they attacked Bosanski Samac. That was done by the Serbian Territorial Defence and by the paramilitary units and the JNA joined in later around 11 o'clock, and the barracks, we would see them because we would clean the barracks and we were able to see the red berets and all those people that used to attack Samac. We could see them at the barracks as well. What way was the co-ordination done and who had to obey to whose orders, I cannot say but they were all there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed at Brcko up until 1st May when the bridge by Gornja was destroyed, the passage from Bosnia into Croatia. We were all awakened by the detonation and the iron door opened after that detonation. The same day, around 2 o'clock, we were put on to the buses and then transferred to the barracks at Bijeljina. There was "Fadil Jahic Spanac". That was the name of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened, what happened when you went to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Bijeljina, first, they took us off the bus, then they lined us up and then they took us into a room up somewhere on the first floor, and then they searched and they singled out somebody from Brcko. He was singled out and he was among us from Samac and, as far as I could hear, that man was killed straightaway, shot. We from Samac, we went up into the barracks on the first floor. We stayed there for about an hour and then we were taken into a gymnasium where we remained for the whole duration of our stay at Bijeljina. While I stayed at Bijeljina, I would very often clean the premises of the barracks so that I could see the monuments to Fadil Jahic Spanac after whom the barracks were named. We were also beaten at Bijeljina. They were doing awful things. They forced me to clean the toilet with my hands, to take everything out, and everything had to be clean and white. There was no way to use any detergent or anything, so you had all this, to take all this with your hands, and they were threatening us. You would see when the Arkan's people come how things would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Bijeljina, was this a JNA barracks as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent that was the JNA barracks because the people who guarded us were also soldiers, JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the JNA soldiers at Bijeljina barracks, was there any other people guarding you or participating at that barracks other than the prisoners, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said at Brcko I saw these members of paramilitary groups, the Red Berets and the Grey Wolves that were at Samac. I did not see them at Bijeljina. They were only the JNA reserve soldiers and the ordinary JNA conscripts. That is what I saw, but they threatened that the Arkan soldiers would come but while I was there I could not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay there at Bijeljina barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there for three days, and then an officer came and he called out six of us from Bosanski Samac and they put us on a helicopter, and when we arrived to the helicopter there were three persons from Bosanski Samac that were already there, Izet Izetbegovic, someone with the second name Dragicevic, Ivo from Hasic and Dr. Miroslav Kedacic. In the middle of the helicopter there was a coffin with mortal remains. The name was there. I cannot remember it exactly, but it started something with "Fuk", either the surname or the first name started with "Fuk". One could see it was a younger man. There was a member from Arkan's unit there, a military man, and somebody, another civilian. Later on I met the civilian when I was at the airfield at Batajnica when they interrogated us. From there we were flown by helicopter to Batajnica. I could see when we were crossing the River Drina and the River Sava, they were threatening us that they would throw us out of the helicopter. We were all attached together and handcuffed. There were eight or nine of us, so in case they would throw one person, all the others would simply follow afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was threatening this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The member of the Arkan's unit who was sitting in front of the coffin and he asked the officer: "When are we going to start to throw them out?" and the officer said: "Wait a while, a little bit later", but they did not even try.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that the helicopter continued to where -- could you repeat it again, where you went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment we did not know, but later on when we landed we realised that we landed on a runway, a runway of an airfield. Then they put us on a truck and then put us into a building and put us in the cellar rooms in that building, and so we could feel we would hear that we were at an airfield because we would constantly hear the landing or the taking off of the planes. That lasted the whole day. For sometime they were hiding it from us where we were, and we were trying among us to find out where we were, at which airfield. Somebody said some Sombor or Batajnica. Later on they told us that we were at Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Batajnica is a military airfield just outside of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "military" do you mean JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was an airfield that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you while you were kept at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The abuse continued, the same type of abuse we used to have in previous camps, the same Chetniks songs. We even had in that camp a drawing of Draza Milhajlvic, the Chetnik commander, that had been sentenced as a war criminal after the Second World War. In the morning when we got up, we had to come nearer and kiss him in his front and say: "Good morning, General". We had to stand from 5 o'clock in the morning till 10 o'clock in the night. We were not allowed to sit down. They were interrogating us and hitting us, abusing -- all these things happened just as in the previous camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were doing this you were being forced to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question, I did not understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you had to do these things, including the kissing of the picture, you were doing it under force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Who would else kiss Draza Mihajlvic? They forced us to do that. Somebody even missed and he kissed him in the lips instead in the full head and said he is not gay to kiss him on his lips. One really had to pay attention where one was kissing the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the nature of the songs that they forced you to sing? What were they about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those songs were celebrating the Serbian people and the combat, and at the same time they were rather inorientated towards the Croats and the Muslims. There was also the text, a song by very popular Croatian singer called Tice which was called "Let's Become Very Foolish this Night", and we had to change the lyrics saying that "Let's be Foolish Tonight and take out the Croatian Eyes", and so on. Me, I as the Chairman of the SDA was forced to sing another, a song against Alija Izetbegovic, saying that Alija Izetbegovic's skin was on a particular mountain and that, so what, because we are going to make cigarette paper out of it. I and Izetbegovic had to sing that song and they said, "The Chairman, you have to sing that song", and while they were beating you they would just say "louder" and "louder" and then the others had to join in and sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were they beating you with when they were forcing you to sing these songs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were beating us at Batajnica with very big batons, big military police batons, and then they forced us to beat one another, to slap one another, and then if you hit him just slightly then they would hit you. Then a policeman would tell you to hit somebody and if you hit that person, then somebody else would hit you and say, "Why are you hitting that person?" So, if you obey somebody then somebody else starts hitting you because you obeyed and then somebody else because you disobeyed.
