Then they would put five chairs, one next to the other, and these chairs you could pass through underneath and then they give you five seconds to pass underneath those five chairs, to take my jug of water then go through two rooms and then have to fill them with water and then come back within five seconds. It was absolutely physically not possible. Then this ill-treatment would last for several hours, where you were running, they would either make you fall or do something else so that you cannot make it. Then when they had enough of it, then they would let you go and then they would count five seconds slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were doing this were you being beaten at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while you were going underneath the chairs they would kick you with his foot on your head or on your back and say, "Hurry up", and while you were carrying the water in case you came across one of them, then they make it seem that you were attacking them and then they would ask you, "Why are you attacking me?" pretending that you wanted to take his rifle or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they interrupt your sleep when you were kept there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. One could never be sure that when you would go to bed at 10 o'clock, go to sleep at 10 o'clock that you could be in peace until 5 o'clock in the morning because somebody would come in and force us to sing songs, one song, two songs, three songs, because they had three-hour shifts and they were bored so they would interrupt things. Sometimes you would not get any sleep, and then the next day from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. you had to stand and you were not allowed to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now on 10th May were you then taken to another place in Serbia? Were you taken to Zemun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not taken to Zemun but other people from my group were taken there, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. What happened to you; what was the next thing that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the meantime while those people were in Zemun, myself and Izet Izetbegovic and Dragicevic, we were taken to the television one day. They were making a programme about the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where this television station was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was somewhere on the premises of the JNA airfield. They were taking us to a building and the cameras had already been there, and there was a journalist, Lazanski, I know him from TV, and he started to ask us various questions. He asked us: How did we drive out Serbs from Samac? I said, no, we did not drive them out; they drove us out because they attacked Samac. Then he said, he asked me: "How did you throw the Serbs out of the police?" I said, "No, that is not correct at all. Out of 20 policemen 12 were Serbs and the rest were the Croatians and Muslims, even the Croats represented the majority of population there." Then somebody would take me and said: "How can you lie? You can't say such things." You see that in all documents and in all reports things should be stated in this way. While I was going out somebody hit me on my head. They asked me all kinds of things, and we would all give answers to it. Obviously you had to say that all the treatment was all right, that nobody was beating us, that the sanitary conditions were good and that we had enough food and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then subsequently learn that you had been tried for crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I am not sure. I heard that somebody stated that I was guilty or that I was a criminal, I do not know what for. I cannot even suppose what for. I was arrested at the very beginning of the war. I can only be their victim, nothing else, because not even later I did not participate actively in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you told that you had been sentenced to death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In fact, that is how it was. One day at Batajnica a soldier came and he gave me newspapers to read. The name of the newspaper was a Belgrade newspaper called Vecernje Novosti. I had to read an article out loud saying that myself, Izet Izetbegovic, Alija Fitozovic and others from Samac, from the SDA, were sentenced by the Muslim side to death. That is what I read, if you mean that, but I knew that was a lie, that was only propaganda, because the Bosnian side had no reason to judge me and try me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then? What was the next thing that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We remained at Batajnica. In the meantime another group arrived to Batajnica. They were from somewhere and there was an American among them and a Croatian soldier. The American and the Croatian soldier were beaten quite a lot. The American all the time while they were beating him, he did not say a word; most people do scream or cry. Somebody told him to extend his hands but he was all the time keeping his hands next to his body, and he realised that, the soldier realised that he knew yoga and that he could not feel pain if he held his hands in that way and when he had to spread out his hands, his arms, then he started screaming as well. So he was beaten quite a lot. The Croatian soldier was beaten quite a lot and they were forced to take the penis one into each other's mouth, and somebody else called Alija was beaten very much and he subsequently the following morning died from the beatings. They accused him he had killed some hundreds of Serbs. They brought him to me. They knew I was a judge and they said: "Now you are a judge you have to sentence him." Then they would ask him: "How many people you killed?" He said: "Hundred". I saw he was completely, completely massacred. Then they start and say: "How many?" Then he said: "A thousand". Then they said: "How many?" and he would say "A million". He was completely out of his mind of those beatings and then the next morning he died. He was handcuffed to somebody else, Bidoric, he moved his hand and realised the other person was dead. They used to use an iron thing that they would put on his fist and then they would kick him on his back. It was unimaginable the way they beat them. When they brought this group there must have been some 50 soldiers, some reservists, they were constantly beating when they brought that American, the Croatian soldier, and that man named Alija. There was also a JNA lieutenant, a Muslim, they imprisoned him, arrested him somewhere and they did the same thing to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From Batajnica where did you then go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Batajnica they transferred us to Sremska Mitrovica. This is a town in Serbia, in Vojvodina. We went to the Sremska Mitrovica prison establishment, penitentiary, that was built by the Austro-Hungarians, and part of it was a military camp of the JNA and that is where we were. When they brought us there, around 1800 hours, they did not stop beating us until 3 o'clock in the morning. We would just fall down unconscious and they would strip us and they would beat us. When you fell unconscious they put you into the room and when you would come round they would take you back. It all lasted until 3 o'clock in the morning. When a captain came I heard that he was a Croat and he stopped those beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you transferred to Sremska Mitrovica on 27th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27th May military policemen came, some other military policemen, not the ones that guarded us, and they handcuffed us and put us in the military pinzgauers van and then they took us from Batajnica to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it regular JNA soldiers who were guarding the prison at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were 100 per cent regular JNA soldiers. While I was there these were all conscripts; not even reservists were there, although the prisoners that I found there, they were prisoners from Vukovar. They told us that there had been some reservists there, but not at that time while I was there. There was only the army. I know because while we were cleaning the officers' building Tito's picture was still hanging there and at one time he was the Commander of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you beaten whilst you were kept at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the first day that was the worst time, we waited between 6 in the afternoon and 3 o'clock the next morning, and then it continued with the beatings. As they would give you lunch -- they would give you breakfast and dinner. Every morning after breakfast there were some 50 of us. As soon as they entered we had to stand up and they would start and beat us on our backs. The ones that were new we were beaten more frequently, later on a bit less. I know that my ribs were broken; I could not sit down. I remember I also urinated blood. These were all huge soldiers. You had to turn towards the wall and then he would run towards you and with a big boot he would hit you, and then if you fell you had to stand up again and he would hit you in the kidneys. It was usually done after breakfast and after dinner. The three of them would enter and out of us 50, roughly speaking, every third one of us would be beaten. We also had to sing the songs there, the same type of songs as previously. They even made a choir out of us. Some of us that were more gifted musically and knew how to sing, we had to sing and lined up and the others were given cloths in order to wave with those cloths. Then they would single out somebody beat, you and you had to continue singing and then they would bring you back to the choir and then you had to sing, continuing singing. When the International Red Cross would arrive, just on that day they would not beat anyone; as soon as they would leave straightaway in the afternoon they would start the beatings again. If somebody would complain to the ICRC they told it to the commander and then the treatment was even worse. Then they had an informer in the room. No matter while members of Red Cross would be just with us, somebody that was in with us would tell it to the others. So after the ICRC would have left they would call that particular person and beat that person even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, what were the conditions like in terms of food and hygiene and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Sremska Mitrovica, as compared with Batajnica, the hygiene was much, much better. We had a toilet and we could go there without having to ask the guard for permission. There was enough water to drink. One could wash one's hands and face. How we could take a bath, that is quite true, once in a fortnight, they would push all 50 of us and while the water was usually either too hot or too cold, but compared with Batajnica where there was nothing or in Samac or Bijeljina or Brcko, it was much better. In Batajnica sometimes 10 days would go by without being able to wash oneself, not to mention some other hygienic needs. So that Mitrovica was better, even though there we could take a bath once in 14 days, but at least one could go to the washroom without having to ask. In other places it was very, the most dangerous thing was to go to the WC, to the loo, because you usually went between the guards and they hit and beat, so one tried to refrain and not go whenever possible. There in Mitrovica they also brought television there; I think it was BBC. One morning the camp commander came and he called out me, Filip Karaula, he was a commander of a part of the front in Vukovar, and a German called Raisner, I think he was called. So he called out our names. We came out. You could stand by the wall, you put your hands behind you and bent your head and you wait for something to say. There were two of them, big ones, with electric truncheons, and one of them said: "I want you to speak for television. I want you to say that nobody beaten you. I want you to say that you have enough food. I want you to say that you have hygiene. Is that clear? he said: "Any questions?" I asked: "Well, can I say that the paramilitaries battered me in Bosnia, that they plundered and robbed me?" He said: "Well, as you like, but don't forget that I can find you even in Rijeka where your family is." It was strange to me how could they know where my family was. So I did not speak about that. Then after that when the cameras were recording us, the camp commander was there and the head of KOS of the Counter Intelligence Service in the camp while we were making our statements were there. So we had to say what we had been asked to, except they allowed us to take a bath in the morning and we shaved so that we could look decently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were cleaned up but you said what they told you to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had to; one could not say anything else. We had to say that the conditions were good. They asked me to invite Alija Izetbegovic to set free some soldiers who allegedly had been captured somewhere in Bosnia, and I did address that invitation to Izetbegovic to release those soldiers, if he had done because then we would also be set free. I was asked to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that the policeman that was standing in guard there when you came in had electric batons. What are they? Can you tell us what they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, we called them "electric batons". I do not know what you call them. They are sticks, they are batons of about 60 centimetres long and when it hits you on the back something like a spring, like a metal spring or like a small bullet or ball comes out and hits you here and it hurts more than the whole of the stick. So it had a spring or something and then a small ball which just jumps out, flies out when the baton touches you and hits you here in the chest and it hurt more than the stick, the baton itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next day, after you gave your statement, were you told anything about the statement that you had given by the people that were keeping you captive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day we were taken out for a walk; even those walks were very few. Then there was the commander, the head of the camp, and they asked this soldier if I could talk to the commander and he approached him and asked him and I was permitted to do so. I said: "Commander, are you satisfied with the statement I gave, I said what you had asked me to?" And he said: "Yes, I am satisfied and our command is satisfied." Then I said: "Well, does it mean that I shall be exchanged together with Croats who were being prepared for exchange, for swapping with the Croatian Army?" And he said: "You're asking me too much", and that was the end of it and I was exchanged. He did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then? What was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, shortly afterwards, two or three days later, there was this big exchange when all the Croatian prisoners who were in Mitrovica and the Bosnian prisoners from Bosnia were made part of that big exchange package, and they took place at Nemetin, but the exchange itself, two days before that we hardly slept at all. We had to clean. We boarded 15 bus and to board the bus meant battery. First we travelled from Mitrovica to Nemetin, it is about 100 kilometres. It took us 12 hours to get there. We stopped in every Serb village and whenever we would stop they would open the doors and they would let in persons, those women, and they would start hitting us and those guards, soldiers rather, military police who were travelling with us, they gave alcohol and they drank. It was such harassment, such mistreatment, such battery, that I did not think that one could survive that. When we arrived in Nemetin the International Red Cross came and said that the exchange was being postponed because the Croats had not brought all, and that I think created even greater fear and the soldiers continued to do whatever they liked; I mean those who wanted they hit us, they beat us. At a certain point in time so many persons had boarded the bus that one did not know who was hitting whom and who was beating whom. There were too many of them. I think they lost consciousness at one point, and when I came I realised that there was peace reigning and since we had to sit bent with our head between our knees and as I was sitting like that I saw somebody walking up and down the bus and I could see that his trousers had some holes or something, that they were strange trousers, and then when I raised my head I saw they were UNPROFOR or something, that is Ukrainians, or rather that we were at the site of exchange. Then from Slavonia people came from Bijeljina and they were also taking vengeance on us, but after that the exchange took place. It took place at Nemetin which is near Osijek in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What date did you leave Sremska Mitrovica? What date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 14th August in the morning about 3 or 4 o'clock. The exchange took place that day around 6 o'clock that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then subsequently medically examined and can you tell us the results of your medical examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Rijeka I went for these examinations, that is X-rays of my bones and ribs, and the scars were an indication that I had three ribs broken, that healed in the meantime, and there were no other fractures. I lost four teeth when they battered me in Samac. But whether there will be some delayed effects I do not know. That is what the physician find out, the fracture of the three ribs, four broken teeth. I felt the effects of kidneys and urinated blood. Now I do not feel, I have no complaints, but I do not know whether something will develop later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For about a month or so after you were released were you unable to sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and there were problems like that. I was afraid to sleep and whenever I went to sleep I dreamt of being in a camp. I dreamt that it was taking place in camp, so when I would wake up I simply could not regain my consciousness. I did not know whether the reality was the dream or whether the dream was the reality; whether I was dreaming I was free or the other way. For about a month I had very serious complaints. I would wake up at night sweating and it would take me about 15 minutes to simply realise that I was free, that I was not in a camp any longer, but it happened more and more seldom and now I have such dreams once in six months or so. But I have got rid of that more or less. I did go to doctors and was told that it simply had to be. They recommended me the therapy to talk about it to give vent to this, and so one gets rid of such problems and that is that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have a question. We have heard from you about paramilitaries, about the JNA. I have not heard anything of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you ever come across members of that army or did that army not exist as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was in Bosanski Samac at that moment there was a Serb police and Serb Territorial Defence. It was not called the Army of the Republika Srpska, but in point of fact there is this forerunner and there were those formations which arrived from Serbia, Grey Wolves, Red Berets. So there was the Serb Territorial Defence which is the forerunner of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Tihic. Izetbegovic whom you mentioned, do you know whether he was related or is related to the President of the same name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are children of two brothers; he and the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina are children of two brothers.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any additional questions, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Mr. Tihic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then you are permanently excused, Mr. Tihic. Thank you for coming. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not sure that our next witness is here. We have been moving with much faster speed, but I think we might have an enquiry made in case the witness was able to be brought down. The witnesses are being kept out of the Hague, not in the city of the Hague. So it is not easy to get them here at very short notice. So I will have an enquiry made just in case the witness was able to be brought. No, unfortunately not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 10 a.m. tomorrow morning.

procedural_notes.text: (The court adjourned for a short time)
(The hearing adjourned until the following day)
